a: Ignatius, also called Theophorus
p: Every letter opens with the same second name: Theophorus, 'God-bearer'.
b: Greek Theophoros, 'God-bearer'. Lake's footnote at Ignatius to the Ephesians 1:0 gives the story told in the third-century Acts of Ignatius: asked who Theophorus is, Ignatius answers, 'He who has Christ in his heart.' See the note at Ignatius to the Romans 1:0.

a: to Polycarp
p: The only one of the seven letters written to one person: the overseer of Smyrna.
b: Polycarp led the church at Smyrna and was put to death there in AD 155 or 156 (Lightfoot); at his trial he said, 'For eighty-six years I have been his slave' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 9:3), and when the fire did not consume him an executioner stabbed him (Martyrdom of Polycarp 16:1); his own letter to the Philippians and the account of his death are on this site (see the topic Polycarp of Smyrna). Eusebius: from Troas Ignatius wrote 'in particular to Polycarp, who led' the church of Smyrna, and 'knowing him very well as an apostolic man, he entrusts to him, as a true and good shepherd, the flock at Antioch' (Church History 3.36.10, the site's translation of the Greek). Lightfoot: Ignatius 'had during his stay in Smyrna received much kindly attention from Polycarp'.
r: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1-2; Martyrdom of Polycarp 9:3; Revelation 2:8-11; Martyrdom of Polycarp 16:1

a: or rather, one overseen by God the Father
p: Ignatius plays on the word: Polycarp oversees the church, but God oversees him.
b: Greek episkopō ... mallon episkopēmenō hypo theou patros. Episkopos is 'overseer', the word behind 'bishop', as in the site's Philippians 1:1; the Plain English Translation keeps 'overseer' so the play shows. Lightfoot compares Paul's turn of phrase, 'now you know God. Better said, God knows you' (Galatians 4:9), and 1 Peter 2:25, where Christ is 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls'. The letter ends on the same word: 'the unity and the oversight of God' (8:3).

a: as on an immovable rock
p: The picture of the house on the rock (Matthew 7:24-25).
b: Greek hōs epi petran akinēton. Lightfoot points to the parable: the sensible man 'built his house on bedrock' (Matthew 7:24-25; Luke 6:48). The same 'firmly settled' (hēdrasmenēn) opens Ignatius to the Philadelphians 1:0.

a: I was counted worthy to see your blameless face
p: Pearson and Lightfoot take this to mean Ignatius first saw Polycarp at Smyrna.
b: Greek kataxiōtheis tou prosōpou sou tou amōmou. Lightfoot: 'having been permitted to see thy face.' He quotes Pearson, 'Numquam igitur ante viderat Polycarpum' (so he had never seen Polycarp before), and calls it 'a just inference', which 'refutes the statement' of the later Antiochene account of the martyrdom that the two had studied together under John. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) still calls Polycarp Ignatius's 'fellow-disciple in the school of St. John'.
orig: καταξιωθεὶς τοῦ προσώπου σου τοῦ ἀμώμου

a: May I have the benefit of it in God
p: Greek onaimen, Ignatius's favorite wish, the verb of Philemon 1:20.
b: Greek hou onaimēn en theō. The Plain English Translation renders onaimēn 'May I have the benefit of' every time (Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:2; 6:2 here). Lightfoot: 'and may I have joy of it'.

a: to put more into your race
p: Greek prostheinai to dromo sou, 'to add to your race'.
b: Lightfoot: 'to run thy race with increased vigour'; the race 'reproduces S. Paul's favourite metaphor of the stadium', as in 'finish my race' (Acts 20:24) and 'I have run the course to the finish' (2 Timothy 4:7). Ignatius speaks to Polycarp as a coach to a runner; the athlete comes in 1:3.

a: Do justice to your place
p: Greek ekdikei sou ton topon: make your office respected by doing it well.
b: Greek ekdikei sou ton topon. Topos, 'place', is a church office here, as in Acts 1:25 (Lightfoot) and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:1 ('Let no one's place puff him up'). Lightfoot: 'vindicate, assert, thine office, i.e. make it felt and respected by a diligent discharge of its duties.' Lake: 'Vindicate your office'. The care is 'of the flesh and of the spirit': the bodily needs of the church and its spiritual ones.
r: Acts 1:25; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 6:1; 1 Timothy 4:12-16

a: Put up with everyone in love
p: Ignatius uses Paul's words to the Ephesians (Lake's margin).
b: Greek pantōn anechou en agapē. Paul: 'Put up with one another in love' (Ephesians 4:2), the verse Lake's margin gives. 'Carry everyone, as the Lord carries you' uses bastazō, the verb of Galatians 6:2 ('Carry each other's heavy loads') and of 1:3.

a: Carry everyone's diseases, as a perfect athlete
p: Polycarp is to do what Matthew 8:17 says Christ did, and to do it like an athlete.
b:
Greek pantōn tas nosous bastaze hōs teleios athlētēs. Lake's margin gives Matthew 8:17: 'He himself took our weaknesses and carried our diseases' (Isaiah 53:4). The overseer is to share his people's troubles as Christ bore theirs. Lightfoot also hears Matthew 5:46-48 in this chapter: 'perfect' as the Father is perfect, and 'If you love good disciples' (2:1) beside 'if you love the people who love you'.

Lake's footnote on 'athlete': 'No other translation is possible: "athlete" was, both then and later, a favourite name for Christians who strove to excel in virtue, especially in ascetic practices'. Lightfoot notes that 1 Clement had already used it (1 Clement 5:1, 'the athletes closest to our own time').
orig: πάντων τὰς νόσους βάσταζε ὡς τέλειος ἀθλητής

a: the way God does
p: Greek kata homoetheian theou, 'with the same character as God'.
b: Greek tois kat' andra kata homoēthian theou lalei, 'to them man by man, in likeness of character with God, speak'. Lake: 'after the manner of God'. Polycarp is to speak to each person by name, as God deals with each one. The Greek manuscript G reads boētheian, 'help', for this rare word; see the variants.

a: that earns you no thanks
t: No thanks for loving the good
p: An echo of Jesus's 'what thanks do you have coming?' (Luke 6:32).
b: Greek charis soi ouk estin. Jesus: 'If you love the people who love you, what thanks do you have coming for that?' (Luke 6:32; compare Matthew 5:46). The overseer's skill is shown with the 'more troublesome' (loimoteroi, literally 'more pestilent').

a: The same plaster does not heal every wound
p: Ignatius pictures the overseer as a doctor who fits the remedy to the patient.
b: Greek ou pan trauma tē autē emplastrō therapeuetai. tous paroxysmous embrochais paue. A plaster was a medicine spread on cloth and laid on a wound; embrochai are wet compresses or fomentations, and paroxysmoi 'sharp pains or fits' (Lightfoot). Lightfoot gives parallels from medical and moral writers for the proverb of the plaster. Ignatius called Christ the 'one doctor' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2).
orig: οὐ πᾶν τραῦμα τῇ αὐτῇ ἐμπλάστρῳ θεραπεύεται

a: Be sharp like the snake in all things
p: Jesus's words to the Twelve, here in the singular to Polycarp.
b: Greek phronimos ginou hōs ho ophis en hapasin kai akeraios eis aei hōs hē peristera. Jesus told the Twelve: 'So be sharp like snakes and pure like doves' (Matthew 10:16). Ignatius puts it in the singular, adds 'in all things' and 'always', and gives each animal the article. Lake's footnote: G leaves out 'the' before 'snake', 'but the parallelism with ἡ περιστερά shows that this is only an accident'.
orig: φρόνιμος γίνου ὡς ὁ ὄφις ἐν ἅπασιν

a: That is why you are made of flesh and of spirit
p: Polycarp's two sides suit two tasks: what is seen and what is not.
b: Greek dia touto sarkikos ei kai pneumatikos, hina ta phainomena sou eis prosōpon kolakeuēs. Lightfoot: kolakeuēs here is 'mayest humour', deal gently with, as the same verb is used of coaxing the beasts in Ignatius to the Romans 4:2 and 5:2. With his flesh Polycarp tends what he can see; with prayer he asks God to show him the rest.
r: Ignatius to the Romans 4:2; Ignatius to the Romans 5:2

a: The time demands you, as pilots demand winds
p: Lake: 'the details are hopelessly obscure. Possibly something has dropped out of the text.'
b: Greek ho kairos apaitei se, hōs kybernētai anemous kai hōs cheimazomenos limena. Lake's footnote: 'The general meaning of this passage is fairly clear, but the details are hopelessly obscure. Possibly something has dropped out of the text.' Lightfoot: the Greek, 'making the crisis the captain and Polycarp the breeze, is certainly not what we should expect'; he conjectures a text in which the hour needs Polycarp as a ship needs its pilot: 'The ship of the Church is tossed to and fro on the ocean of the world.' The Plain English Translation follows Lake's Greek.
orig: ὡς κυβερνῆται ἀνέμους καὶ ὡς χειμαζόμενος λιμένα

a: The prize is incorruption and eternal life
p: Greek thema, the cash prize of the games, set beside 'incorruption'.
b: Greek to thema aphtharsia kai zōē aiōnios. Lake's footnote: 'thema means a "money-prize," which was given in some of the Greek games instead of the stephanos or crown.' Lightfoot cites inscriptions with the word from Aphrodisias, Ephesus, Troas and Thyatira. Paul uses the crown (1 Corinthians 9:25); Ignatius uses the purse, and fills it with 'incorruption'.
orig: τὸ θέμα ἀφθαρσία καὶ ζωὴ αἰώνιος

a: I am a life in exchange for you
p: Greek antipsychon, 'a life given for another': Ignatius offers his death for Polycarp.
b: Greek kata panta sou antipsychon egō kai ta desma mou. The Plain English Translation renders antipsychon 'a life in exchange' here, at 6:1 and in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 10:2, as in 4 Maccabees 6:29. Lake: 'I am devoted to you'. Lightfoot refers to his note on Ignatius to the Ephesians 21.
r: 4 Maccabees 6:29; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 10:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 21:1; 6:1

a: Stand firm like a struck anvil
p: An anvil does not move under the hammer: so the overseer under attack.
b: Greek stēthi hedraios hōs akmōn typtomenos. Lightfoot quotes the Greek of Job 41, where the monster 'stands like an anvil', and classical uses of the picture. 'A great athlete takes the blows and wins': deresthai is literally 'to be flayed', the beating a fighter takes. The danger is 'those who seem trustworthy but teach something different' (heterodidaskalountes, the verb of 1 Timothy 1:3 and 6:3, 'teach anything different').

a: the timeless, the invisible, visible for our sake
p: A chain of opposites: timeless, unseen, untouchable, beyond suffering, yet seen and suffering for us.
b:
Greek ton hyper kairon prosdoka, ton achronon, ton aoraton, ton di' hēmas horaton, ton apsēlaphēton, ton apathē, ton di' hēmas pathēton. 'Beyond suffering' and 'able to suffer' (apathē, pathēton) are the pair of Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2 ('first able to suffer and then beyond suffering'). Lightfoot notes that there is no balancing 'touchable for our sake': 'The preponderance of authority forbids the insertion', and 'the run of the sentence is against it'.

Lightfoot sees in this chapter 'a passing allusion expressed in general terms' to the heresy that fills the companion letter, Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans, whose teachers said Christ suffered only in appearance (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1). Read that way, the one beyond time and suffering truly suffered 'for our sake'. Lightfoot also notes that the pairs of opposites have parallels in later writers. Compare 1 John 1:1, the word of life 'our hands touched'.
orig: τὸν ἄχρονον, τὸν ἀόρατον, τὸν δι᾽ ἡμᾶς ὁρατόν
r: Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1; John 1:14; Colossians 1:15; 1 Timothy 1:17; 1 John 1:1

a: The widows must not be neglected
p: The overseer is to be the widows' guardian 'after the Lord'.
b: Greek chērai mē ameleisthōsan; meta ton kyrion sy autōn phrontistēs eso. The New Testament makes widows a charge of the church (Acts 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16; James 1:27). Here the overseer himself is their 'caretaker'. Ignatius greets 'the virgins who are called widows' at Smyrna (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:1). See the topic Widows.
r: Acts 6:1; 1 Timothy 5:3-16; James 1:27; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:1

a: Let gatherings be held more often
p: Greek synagogai, the word behind 'synagogue', of the church's meetings.
b: Greek pyknoteron synagōgai ginesthōsan. James uses the same word of a church meeting (James 2:2). Ignatius urged the Ephesians too 'to come together more often for the thanksgiving' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1). 'Seek out everyone by name': the overseer knows his people one by one (compare John 10:3, 3 John 1:14).
r: James 2:2; Hebrews 10:25; Ignatius to the Ephesians 13:1; John 10:3; 3 John 1:14

a: Do not look down on male and female slaves
p: What the verse says, what it does not say, and how it has been read.
b:
Greek mē eratōsan apo tou koinou eleutherousthai, hina mē douloi heurethōsin epithymias. Slaves must not be looked down on, nor be 'puffed up'; they should serve 'for the glory of God', hoping for 'a better freedom from God', and should not long to be freed from the common fund.

Lightfoot reads to koinon as 'the common fund, the public money', points to the Apostolic Constitutions (4.9), where church money frees slaves, and explains the warning by the fund's limits. He rejects Zahn's 'the community': with this verb 'we should certainly expect hypo tou koinou, not apo tou koinou'. 'Let them serve all the more' is, he says, 'a reminiscence' of 1 Timothy 6:2 ('serve them better still', Lake's margin), said here of all slaves. He also compares 1 Corinthians 7:21 'according to one, though not the most probable, interpretation'; the site's note there sets out both readings.

This is Lightfoot's reading (see the chapter page). On how the churches read Scripture on slavery, see the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon.
orig: μὴ ἐράτωσαν ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ ἐλευθεροῦσθαι

a: Run from the evil arts
p: The same words as Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:2: the schemes of false teachers, or magic.
b: Greek tas kakotechnias pheuge, mallon de peri toutōn homilian poiou. Lightfoot: the meaning 'is shown by the parallel passage', Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:2, 'the schismatical designs of the false teachers'; the word was used 'especially of "magical arts"', and Hilgenfeld took it so here. Homilia is a talk or sermon, the word behind 'homily': Polycarp is not only to avoid them but to preach against them. Lightfoot sees him doing so in Irenaeus's memory of him.
r: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 6:2; Acts 19:19; Galatians 5:20

a: love their wives as the Lord loves the church
p: Ignatius echoes Paul's charge to husbands.
b: Greek agapan tas symbious hōs ho kyrios tēn ekklēsian. Paul: 'Husbands, love your wives in the way Christ loved the church' (Ephesians 5:25) and 'as Christ also does for the church' (Ephesians 5:29). Lake's margin points to Ephesians 5:25; Lightfoot calls it 'A reminiscence of Ephes. v. 29'. The word for husband and wife is symbios, 'life-partner'; Lightfoot thinks it may have been 'especially welcome' to Christians because it covered the unions of slaves, which Roman law did not count as marriage.

a: If anyone is able to remain in purity
p: Ignatius welcomes the single life, but only with humility and with the overseer's knowledge.
b:
Greek ei tis dynatai en hagneia menein eis timēn tēs sarkos tou kyriou, en akauchēsia menetō. Hagneia is 'purity' (Lake 'continence'): here, staying unmarried. Lightfoot: 'the flesh, the body, of the Lord' is explained by 1 Corinthians 6:15, where believers' bodies are Christ's members. 'If it becomes known beyond the overseer' is, he says, the person's 'purpose or vow of chastity': it is shared with the overseer but no one else, so that 'the precept of Ignatius thus contrasts with the usage of a later age, where the public profession of such vows was an essential feature'. He sees 'no indication here of an "order" of virgins'. He rejects the rendering 'if he be better known than the bishop' as not 'at all a natural expression in the present context'. Lake: 'if it be made known except to the bishop'; on the Greek word behind 'beyond' see the variants.

The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), a reference work rather than a church document, cites this chapter for 'the supernatural virtue of virginity, already much esteemed and made the subject of a vow'. Paul's words on the single life are 1 Corinthians 7:7-8 and 7:32-35; on how the churches differ about vows and the single life, see the cards at 1 Corinthians 7 and Matthew 19:12.
orig: εἴ τις δύναται ἐν ἁγνείᾳ μένειν

a: Men and women who marry should make their union with the overseer's approval
p: A rule tying marriage to the church's leader: what it says, and how it is read.
b:
Greek prepei de tois gamousi kai tais gamoumenais meta gnōmēs tou episkopou tēn henōsin poieisthai, hina ho gamos ē kata kyrion kai mē kat' epithymian. Lake: 'it is right for men and women who marry to be united with the consent of the bishop'. Ignatius gives the reason: so that the marriage 'may follow the Lord and not desire'. Lightfoot paraphrases: 'Let those who marry seek the approval of the bishop for their union'; he thinks Ignatius has Paul's 'only in the Lord' in mind (1 Corinthians 7:39), and refers for 'the sanction given by the Church to marriages in the early ages' to Probst and Bingham. The verse asks for the overseer's approval; it says nothing of a ceremony or of who must perform it.

The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), a reference work rather than a church document, lists the chapter as a witness to 'the religious character of matrimony'. Whether marriage is a sacrament is the question of the card at Ephesians 5:32; on marrying unbelievers see 2 Corinthians 6 and Ezra 10; on divorce, Matthew 19 and 1 Corinthians 7.
orig: μετὰ γνώμης τοῦ ἐπισκόπου τὴν ἕνωσιν ποιεῖσθαι

a: Pay attention to the overseer, so that God may pay attention to you
p: Here the 'you' becomes plural: Ignatius turns from Polycarp to the church.
b: Greek tō episkopō prosechete, hina kai ho theos hymin. The verb is plural. Lightfoot: 'Ignatius here turns from Polycarp individually and addresses the whole Church of Smyrna', and 'Like the Pastoral Epistles of S. Paul, this letter was obviously intended to be made known to the Church also.' From here on, he notes, Ignatius names Polycarp when he means him alone (7:2; 8:2).
r: Hebrews 13:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:12-13; Ignatius to the Philadelphians 7:1

a: Toil together with one another
p: Six verbs each built with syn-, 'together': the church as one team.
b: Greek synkopiate allēlois, synathleite, syntrechete, sympaschete, synkoimasthe, synegeiresthe. Each verb begins with syn-, 'with': toil, compete (the athlete's word), run, suffer, rest, rise, all together. The Plain English Translation keeps all six with 'together'. Lake: 'Labour with one another, struggle together, run together, suffer together, rest together, rise up together'. Lightfoot takes the athlete's training to run through the list: the last two verbs 'refer to the uniform hours of going to bed and getting up prescribed by the trainer to the athletes under his charge', and 'Any reference to "death" and "resurrection" ... seems altogether out of place.'

a: God's stewards, those who sit at his side, and his assistants
p: Three words for the whole church's service, not only its ministers'.
b: Greek hōs theou oikonomoi kai paredroi kai hypēretai. Paul: 'let a person count us as assistants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries' (1 Corinthians 4:1), where the site renders hypēretai 'assistants', as here. Lake has 'stewards and assessors and servants'. Paredroi are those who sit beside a judge or ruler to advise; Lightfoot: 'assessors' of God, 'a stronger expression even than S. Paul's Θεοῦ συνεργοί' (1 Corinthians 3:9), 'immediately qualified by ὑπηρέται'. He holds that the words apply 'to the whole brotherhood', as in 1 Peter 4:10, not to three orders of ministers as Pearson thought.
orig: θεοῦ οἰκονόμοι καὶ πάρεδροι καὶ ὑπηρέται

a: Let none of you be found a deserter
p: Ignatius borrows three Latin words of the Roman army.
b: Greek desertōr, deposita, accepta, written in Greek letters. Lake's footnote: 'The use of the Latin words is remarkable'. Lightfoot: borrowing is 'natural in technical and more especially in military terms', and from Ignatius, 'who was in charge of a στρατιωτικὸν τάγμα and bound to a soldier night and day' (compare the 'ten leopards' of Ignatius to the Romans 5:1), 'nothing else was to be expected'. The verse opens with the soldier's 'pay' (opsōnia), as in 1 Corinthians 9:7, and 'Please the one you serve as soldiers' echoes 2 Timothy 2:4 (Lake's margin).
r: 2 Timothy 2:3-4; 1 Corinthians 9:7; Ignatius to the Romans 5:1

a: Let your baptism remain as your weapons
p: Like Ephesians 6:13-17, but with the pieces given out differently.
b:
Greek to baptisma hymōn menetō hōs hopla, hē pistis hōs perikephalaia, hē agapē hōs dory, hē hypomonē hōs panoplia. Lightfoot: the passage 'was doubtless suggested by Ephes. vi. 13-17, which it closely resembles, though the parts of the armour are differently assigned'. In Paul faith is the shield and salvation the helmet (Ephesians 6:16-17); in 1 Thessalonians 5:8 faith and love are the breastplate and hope the helmet. Here baptism is the hopla, which Lightfoot takes as 'shields', faith the helmet, love the spear.

'Full armor' is panoplia, the word the site renders 'all of God's armor' in Ephesians 6:11 and 6:13; Lightfoot: 'the complete body-armour', since 'Patience protects the whole spiritual man'.

Syriac and Armenian witnesses have a different list here: 'let faith remain with you as arms, and hope as a helmet' (see the variants).
orig: τὸ βάπτισμα ὑμῶν μενέτω ὡς ὅπλα

a: Let your deeds be your deposits
p: Half of a soldier's bonus was banked with the standards and paid at discharge.
b: Greek ta deposita hymōn ta erga hymōn, hina ta accepta hymōn axia komisēsthe. Lake's footnote: 'It was the custom in the Roman army to pay to the soldiers only the half of any gratuities allowed them. The other half was "deposited" in a regimental savings bank, and was paid out to each soldier, when, and if, he was honourably discharged from the service.' Lightfoot adds that a deserter forfeited it all, and quotes Vegetius: the soldier who knows his savings are with the standards 'never thinks of deserting'. The good works of the Christian are savings God pays out at the end.
orig: τὰ δεπόσιτα ὑμῶν τὰ ἔργα ὑμῶν

a: The church in Antioch of Syria is at peace
p: As in the other letters from Troas, news of peace at Antioch.
b: Greek hē ekklēsia hē en Antiocheia tēs Syrias eirēneuei. The same news is in Ignatius to the Philadelphians 10:1 and Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2. Ignatius is 'more cheerful': his own church is safe, and he can go to his death 'in the freedom from care that God gives'.
orig: ἡ ἐκκλησία ἡ ἐν Ἀντιοχείᾳ τῆς Συρίας εἰρηνεύει
r: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 10:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2; Acts 11:19-26

a: if only through suffering I may reach God
p: Lightfoot hears the Greek proverb 'suffering teaches' in 'suffer ... disciple'.
b: Greek eanper dia tou pathein theou epitychō, eis to heurethēnai me ... mathētēn. 'Reach God' is the verb the Plain English Translation uses throughout the letters (Ignatius to the Romans 1:2). Lightfoot: Ignatius 'probably has in his mind the proverb παθήματα μαθήματα' ('sufferings are lessons'), which Hebrews 5:8 also echoes: 'he learned obedience from what he suffered'.
r: Hebrews 5:8; Ignatius to the Romans 1:2; Ignatius to the Romans 5:3

a: to call together a council most fit for God
t: A council to elect an envoy
p: Polycarp is to call the church together to choose its messenger by vote.
b: Greek symboulion agagein theoprepestaton kai cheirotonēsai tina. The overseer calls the council; the church elects (the verb of Acts 14:23 and 2 Corinthians 8:19, 'voted'; see the note at Ignatius to the Philadelphians 10:1). Polycarp's own letter shows he expected to send an envoy: 'If anyone goes to Syria, he should carry the letter from you as well. I will do this if I get a good opportunity, either myself or someone I send as an envoy' (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1). Lightfoot: Polycarp 'refers to this intended delegate'. On who chooses ministers, see the card at Acts 14:23.
r: Acts 14:23; 2 Corinthians 8:19; Acts 15:22; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1

a: God's runner
p: Greek theodromos: here the messenger who will run to Syria.
b: Greek hos dynēsetai theodromos kaleisthai. The word is the 'God's runners' of Ignatius to the Philadelphians 2:2, there of Christians in the race of faith; here, Lightfoot says, it is used 'in reference to the special mission', 'God's courier' (Lake). In Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2 the same messenger is an 'envoy of God'. Lightfoot thinks Lucian mocks such directions in his Death of Peregrinus 41, where the former Christian Peregrinus sends letters to the cities by envoys he calls 'death-messengers and underworld-runners' (nekrangelous kai nerterodromous).
r: Ignatius to the Philadelphians 2:2; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2

a: No Christian has authority over himself
p: Greek Christianos, the name of Acts 11:26, first used at Antioch.
b: Greek Christianos heautou exousian ouk echei, alla theō scholazei. The disciples 'were first called Christians' at Antioch (Acts 11:26), Ignatius's own city. 'Spends his time on God' is the verb of 1:3 ('Make time for prayer'); Lightfoot: 'devotes his time to God'. Compare 1 Corinthians 6:19-20, 'You are not your own'.

a: My sudden sailing from Troas to Neapolis
p: The guards sailed suddenly for Macedonia, Paul's route of Acts 16.
b: Greek dia to exaiphnēs plein me apo Trōados eis Neapolin. Lake's footnote: Neapolis is 'The modern Cavalla, on the coast of Macedonia, between Constantinople and Salonica; the Roman road comes down to the sea there'. Lightfoot: it was 'The port-town of Philippi (Acts xvi. 11), where he would take the great Egnatian road'. Paul made the same crossing: 'Setting off from Troas, we ran a straight course to Samothrace, and on the next day to Neapolis' (Acts 16:11). Ignatius's next stop, Philippi, is where Polycarp later sent the collected letters (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2).
r: Acts 16:11-12; Acts 20:5-6; Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2

a: as the will of God requires
p: The Greek says only 'the will'; Lightfoot and Lake take it as God's.
b: Greek hōs to thelēma prostassei. Lightfoot: 'the Divine will'; 'There is no reason for departing from the ordinary use of Ignatius, and explaining it here of the will of the emperor or the Roman authorities', as the Roberts-Donaldson English does ('as the will [of the emperor] enjoins'). Lake: 'as the will of God enjoins'. The Plain English Translation supplies 'of God' with them.

a: so that you may be glorified
p: Lake: 'Modern English obscures the fact that this "you" is plural.'
b: Greek hina doxasthēte aiōniō ergō, plural, while 'you must write' and 'as you are worthy' are singular. Lake's English footnote: 'Modern English obscures the fact that this "you" is plural. The others are singular.' His Greek footnote: 'The combination of singular and plural is very strange. L makes all singular, A all plural. The punctuation given is in the main Lightfoot's, but even so the sentence is unsatisfactory.' Lightfoot takes the bracketed words as an aside and 'as you are worthy' of Polycarp. The 'churches ahead' are those 'nearer to Syria than Smyrna itself' (Lightfoot).

a: the wife of the procurator
p: Greek ten tou Epitropou: 'the woman of Epitropus' or 'of the procurator'.
b: Greek tēn tou Epitropou, with no noun for 'wife': the Plain English Translation supplies it with Lake. Epitropos is a Roman official's title, 'procurator' or 'steward', and might also be a man's name. Lake: 'the wife of the Procurator', with the footnote 'Or, perhaps, "of Epitropus."' Lightfoot prefers 'the widow, rather than the wife', because of the household and children that follow, finds the name Epitropus rare, mentions procurators in inscriptions at Smyrna, and thinks she is 'not improbably the same' as the Tavia (Gavia) of Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:2. The Roberts-Donaldson English has 'the wife of Epitropus'.

a: Attalus
p: A common name at Smyrna; nothing more is known of him.
b: Lightfoot: 'This name appears many times in inscriptions and coins belonging to Smyrna'. Ignatius calls him 'my beloved'.

a: with Polycarp who sends him
p: The messenger to Syria is sent by Polycarp.
b: Lightfoot notes that Cureton's Syriac abridgment, having cut chapter 7, rewrote this line as 'him that is thought worthy to go to Antioch in my stead, as I commanded thee', which could suggest Ignatius's successor as bishop; Lightfoot sees 'no reason to think that the epitomator himself intended this', only 'a piece of slovenly wording'. In Polycarp's own letter he offers to go himself or send someone (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1).

a: Remain in him
p: The letter ends where it began, with God as overseer.
b: Greek en henotēti theou kai episkopē. Lightfoot: 'He had begun the letter by speaking of Polycarp as ἐπεσκοπημένος ὑπὸ Θεοῦ', so there is 'much propriety in his ending with' God's oversight (episkopē). The Armenian read 'of the overseer'; Lightfoot keeps episkopē because the change to 'overseer' 'would be so much more natural to a transcriber than the converse'.

a: I greet Alce, a name dear to me
p: Greeted in the same words in Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:2; perhaps the Alce of the Martyrdom.
b: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:2 has the same words: 'I greet Alce, a name dear to me'. The Martyrdom of Polycarp names 'Nicetes, Herod's father and the brother of Alce', who urged the governor not to give up Polycarp's body (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2). Lightfoot sees 'no difficulty, though a period of forty or fifty years may have elapsed, in supposing the same person to be meant', a family divided over Christ (Matthew 10:35). The texts themselves say only that both women bore the name.
orig: ἀσπάζομαι Ἄλκην, τὸ ποθητόν μοι ὄνομα
r: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 13:2; Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2; Matthew 10:35
